item.title: EU advisers warn bloc unprepared for worsening climate change
item.description:
The European Union is unprepared for worsening climate change and must urgently increase investment to protect people and infrastructure from intensifying floods, wildfires, and severe heatwaves, independent scientific advisers warned on Monday.

The European Scientific Advisory Board on Climate Change released a report titled "Strengthening resilience to climate change – Recommendations for an effective EU adaptation policy framework," calling for a more coordinated approach across member states as the bloc faces escalating climate risks that could "undermine the EU's economic and social foundations."

item.title: Kremlin rejects European findings that Russia poisoned Navalny
item.description:
Scientists and chemical weapons experts conclude that the rare neurotoxin found in Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny's body was almost certainly synthesized in a laboratory rather than harvested from South American dart frogs, according to analysis released at the Munich Security Conference last week.

The United Kingdom, France, Germany, Sweden, and the Netherlands announced on February 14 that laboratory testing had "conclusively confirmed" the presence of epibatidine in samples taken from Navalny's body. The toxin, naturally occurring only in Ecuadorian poison dart frogs, was described as "highly likely" the cause of his death in an Arctic penal colony on February 16, 2024.

item.title: Japan to ship carbon emissions to Malaysia in regional first
item.description:
Japan will ship carbon dioxide emissions to Malaysia in what would be the first cross-border carbon capture and storage project in Southeast Asia, a plan that is drawing criticism from climate advocates who argue the technology is more symbolic than effective in combating climate change.

Under the arrangement, emissions from Japan's polluting industries—including electric power, oil refining, cement, and steel—would be captured, liquefied, and transported by ship to depleted gas fields off the coast of Sarawak on the island of Borneo. If successful, experts say the project could pave the way for similar initiatives in other Southeast Asian nations such as Indonesia and Thailand.

item.title: Experts say toxin that killed Navalny was lab-made, not from frogs
item.description:
The toxin that European governments say killed Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny was almost certainly manufactured in a laboratory rather than extracted from poison dart frogs in the wild, according to experts who spoke out this week following an announcement from five European nations.

Days after the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Sweden, and the Netherlands jointly declared that Navalny was poisoned with epibatidine, a neurotoxin found naturally in South American dart frogs, specialists in amphibian biology and toxicology told news outlets that obtaining the substance from live frogs would be practically impossible.

item.title: Chinese humanoid robots perform kung fu at world's most-watched TV gala
item.description:
China's biggest technology firms used the Lunar New Year holiday to demonstrate the country's growing dominance in artificial intelligence and robotics, with humanoid robots performing martial arts on the world's most-watched television broadcast and several leading AI developers unveiling new flagship models.

Four robotics startups—Unitree Robotics, Galbot, Noetix, and MagicLab—displayed their humanoid machines during the 2026 Spring Festival Gala on Sunday, a China Central Television event comparable in cultural significance to the Super Bowl in the United States. The gala attracted an estimated 79% of live television viewers in China last year, according to Reuters.

item.title: US and Iran begin second round of nuclear talks in Geneva
item.description:
European stocks held firm on Tuesday as investors monitored the second round of nuclear negotiations between the United States and Iran in Geneva, with energy markets also showing stability despite heightened regional tensions.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 was steady in early trading, according to Reuters, as the talks between Washington and Tehran got underway. U.S. markets remained closed for the Presidents' Day holiday, limiting trading volumes across global exchanges.

item.title: Satellite imagery confirms USS Abraham Lincoln near Iran
item.description: As diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran resume in Geneva this week, the Pentagon has assembled what analysts describe as one of the largest American naval concentrations in the Middle East since the 2025 strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities. President Trump has ordered the USS Gerald R. Ford, the Navy's largest and most advanced warship, to join the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group already positioned in the Arabian Sea, creating a rare dual-carrier presence aimed at pressuring Tehran into nuclear concessions.

item.title: Iran begins Strait of Hormuz military drills ahead of US talks
item.description:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched extensive naval exercises in the Strait of Hormuz on February 16, demonstrating its military capabilities just one day before a critical round of nuclear negotiations with the United States in Geneva. The drills, titled "Smart Control of Hormuz Strait," were supervised by IRGC Commander Major General Mohammad Pakpour and aimed to test operational readiness against what Tehran described as "potential security and military threats," according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.

The Strait of Hormuz, located between Oman and Iran, represents one of the world's most critical energy chokepoints. Approximately 20 million barrels of oil flow through the waterway daily, accounting for roughly 20% of global petroleum consumption, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. More than 80% of that crude oil is destined for Asian markets, with China, India, Japan, and South Korea as the primary recipients.

item.title: Scientists drill deepest-ever sediment core under Antarctic ice
item.description:
An international team of researchers has drilled a 228-meter sediment core from beneath the West Antarctic Ice Sheet, setting a record for the deepest geological sample ever retrieved from under any ice sheet. The core, which could span 23 million years of climate history, will help scientists predict how much ice may melt as the planet warms.

The achievement, announced this week by the SWAIS2C (Sensitivity of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet to 2°C) project, came on the team's third attempt after two previous Antarctic seasons were thwarted by technical challenges. The core was extracted from a location at Crary Ice Rise on the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf, more than 700 kilometers from the nearest Antarctic research stations.

item.title: US and Iran begin second round of nuclear talks in Geneva
item.description:
The United States and Iran began a second round of indirect nuclear negotiations in Geneva on Tuesday, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi leading Tehran's delegation following a meeting with the head of the United Nations nuclear watchdog.

The talks, mediated by Oman, come as the U.S. military bolsters its presence in the Middle East and Iran conducts live-fire exercises in the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: Iran temporarily closes parts of Strait of Hormuz during drills
item.description:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards closed sections of the Strait of Hormuz for several hours on Tuesday as the country conducted live-fire naval exercises, marking the first time Tehran has announced a restriction on the critical waterway since the United States began threatening military action and deploying forces to the region in January.

The partial closure coincided with a second round of indirect nuclear talks between the United States and Iran in Geneva, in what analysts described as a demonstration of leverage as Tehran seeks to extract concessions from Washington while negotiations remain fragile.

item.title: Amazon rainforest became a carbon source in 2023, study finds
item.description:
The world's largest rainforest reversed its role as a carbon absorber during 2023's extreme drought, releasing millions of tons of carbon into the atmosphere instead of storing it, according to new research from the Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry.

The study, published this week in AGU Advances, found that the Amazon released between 10 and 170 million tons of carbon in 2023, accounting for roughly 30 percent of net carbon emissions from all tropical lands that year. The findings underscore growing concerns that climate change and deforestation may be pushing the Amazon toward a permanent tipping point.

item.title: Iran and US agree on 'guiding principles' in Geneva nuclear talks
item.description:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held discussions with International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi in Geneva on Monday, hours before resuming indirect nuclear negotiations with the United States. The meeting addressed technical nuclear issues as the UN watchdog continues pressing Tehran for clarity on its uranium stockpile and access to facilities damaged in US and Israeli strikes last year.

Grossi confirmed the session on social media platform X, writing that he had completed "in-depth technical discussions" with Araghchi "in preparation for important negotiations scheduled for tomorrow." The encounter took place at Araghchi's accommodation in Geneva, according to Iran's Foreign Ministry, which stated the two exchanged views on cooperation between Iran and the IAEA within the framework of safeguards obligations.

item.title: UK MPs to consider investigation into Andrew over Epstein leaks
item.description:
British Members of Parliament could launch an investigation into Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's decade-long tenure as a UK trade envoy as early as next week, after newly released documents from the U.S. Justice Department revealed he allegedly shared confidential government briefings with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Liam Byrne, chairman of the cross-party Business and Trade Committee, told reporters on Monday that "nothing is off the table" as lawmakers prepare to consider how to proceed when they meet next Tuesday. The development marks a major escalation in scrutiny of the former prince, who already faces a police assessment over potential misconduct in public office.

item.title: India confirms seizure of Iran-linked tankers, deploys 55 ships
item.description: India has seized three US-sanctioned oil tankers suspected of ties to Iran's shadow fleet, confirming the country's first major enforcement action against vessels evading international sanctions. The operation, which comes amid improving US-India relations following a bilateral trade deal, has prompted an expanded maritime surveillance effort by the Indian Coast Guard.

item.title: Ukraine hits Russian oil refinery as peace talks open in Geneva
item.description:
Ukrainian drones struck multiple regions across Russia overnight on February 17, targeting oil infrastructure and triggering airport closures in what Russian-installed authorities in Crimea described as one of the longest attacks in recent times. The wave of strikes came as Russian and Ukrainian delegations convened in Geneva for a new round of U.S.-brokered peace talks.

Russia's Defense Ministry reported that air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 151 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight, with strikes reaching deep into Russian territory. The attacks targeted regions from Crimea in the south to Tatarstan in central Russia, approximately 1,300 kilometers from the front lines.

item.title: Trump says he's discussing Taiwan arms sales with Xi
item.description:
President Donald Trump acknowledged he has been in direct discussions with Chinese President Xi Jinping regarding US weapons sales to Taiwan, telling reporters aboard Air Force One on February 16 that he would reach a decision "pretty soon." The admission has drawn scrutiny from foreign policy observers, as it appears to contradict the Reagan-era Six Assurances, which commit Washington not to consult with Beijing on arms transfers to the self-governing island.

"I'm talking to him about it. We had a good conversation, and we'll make a determination pretty soon," Trump said, emphasizing his "good relationship" with Xi ahead of a planned April summit in Beijing.

item.title: Anthropic launches Claude Sonnet 4.6 with 1M token context window
item.description:
Anthropic unveiled Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Tuesday, bringing its most capable mid-tier AI model to users across all subscription levels, including free accounts. The release arrives just weeks after the company launched its flagship Opus 4.6 model in early February.

The updated Sonnet model delivers advances in coding, computer use, long-context reasoning, and agent planning. Most notably, it introduces a 1 million token context window in beta, allowing the model to process entire codebases, lengthy contracts, or dozens of research papers in a single request.

item.title: Emails reveal Epstein called himself 'Davos concierge' for elites
item.description:
Jeffrey Epstein leveraged the World Economic Forum's annual gathering in Switzerland to trade influence and arrange meetings between some of the world's most powerful figures, despite claiming to "hate" the forum, according to emails released by the U.S. Department of Justice and a trove of messages from Epstein's Yahoo account obtained by Bloomberg.

The disgraced financier, who died in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges, described himself as a "Davos concierge," offering to help contacts navigate the exclusive conference by securing accommodations in a venue where lodging is scarce and promising to arrange meetings with billionaires and government officials, Bloomberg reported Monday. It remains unclear how many times, if at all, Epstein actually attended the event — the World Economic Forum declined to comment on the matter.

item.title: Oil tanker breaks Cuba's five-week fuel drought amid US blockade
item.description:
The tanker Nicos I.V. entered Cuba's Matanzas Bay on February 16, becoming the first vessel to deliver fuel to the island in more than five weeks as the country struggles through its worst energy crisis since the collapse of the Soviet Union.

The 183-meter vessel, flying the flag of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, docked at Cuba's main energy logistics hub appearing partially loaded, according to maritime monitoring data and reports from El Independiente. While the ship has capacity for more than 300,000 barrels, neither the type nor volume of fuel it carried has been disclosed. If confirmed to have originated from a foreign port, it would be the first international delivery since the Ocean Mariner arrived from Mexico on January 9 with approximately 85,000 barrels, Bloomberg reported at the time.
